questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant has a thick yellow, adherent, greasy scale over the scalp. The infant is comfortable and does not scratch. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Infantile seborrheic dermatitis (cradle cap)
questions.initialExplanation: Infantile seborrheic dermatitis commonly begins in the first months of life with yellow, greasy, adherent scalp scale and usually little or no itch.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Seborrheic dermatitis — Correct. Cradle cap is characterized by thick yellow scale on an erythematous scalp, often without significant discomfort.
- B. Atopic eczema — Incorrect. It is usually itchy and often affects cheeks or extensor surfaces in infants.
- C. Tinea capitis — Incorrect. This typically causes scalp scaling with hair loss or broken hairs and may produce inflammatory lesions.

- D. Scabies — Incorrect. Scabies causes intense itch, often worse at night, with papules/burrows and affected contacts.
- E. Impetigo — Incorrect. This produces superficial bacterial lesions with honey-colored crusts or bullae.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cradle cap: first months of life, greasy yellow adherent scale, usually not itchy.
- It may involve face, behind ears, flexures, or napkin area.
- Usually resolves spontaneously; reassure and use gentle skin care.

questions.stem: Which clinical feature most strongly favors atopic eczema over infantile seborrheic dermatitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Marked pruritus with scratching and excoriation

options.label: B
options.text: Thick yellow greasy scalp scale without itch

questions.correctAnswerText: Marked pruritus with scratching and excoriation
questions.initialExplanation: Pruritus is a key feature of atopic eczema and drives the itch-scratch cycle, whereas infantile seborrheic dermatitis is often not itchy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pruritus and excoriation — Correct. Itching and scratching are central features of atopic eczema.
- B. Yellow greasy scalp scale — Incorrect. This favors seborrheic dermatitis.
- C. Umbilicated papule — Incorrect. This is typical of molluscum contagiosum.

- D. Unperturbed infant — Incorrect. This is typical of cradle cap rather than itchy atopic eczema.
- E. After puberty — Incorrect. Atopic eczema commonly begins in infancy or childhood.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Atopic eczema: itch, dry skin, relapsing inflammation, excoriations/lichenification.
- Distribution varies with age.
- Ask about personal/family history of atopy.

questions.stem: Which distribution is typical of atopic eczema in an older child?

options.label: A
options.text: the scalp with greasy yellow scale

options.label: D
options.text: Skin folds spared with a sharply demarcated napkin rash

questions.correctAnswerText: Flexural areas and friction surfaces
questions.initialExplanation: Atopic eczema changes distribution with age; older children commonly have flexural involvement, while infants often have facial and extensor involvement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Greasy scalp scale — Incorrect. This suggests seborrheic dermatitis.
- B. Dermatomal vesicles — Incorrect. This suggests herpes zoster.
- C. Flexural areas — Correct. Flexures such as the antecubital and popliteal fossae are common sites in older children.
- D. Fold-sparing napkin rash — Incorrect. This is more characteristic of irritant diaper dermatitis.

- E. Palms/soles only — Incorrect. This is not the usual distribution.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infant: cheeks, scalp, trunk/extensor surfaces may be involved.
- Older child: flexural surfaces commonly affected.
- Chronic scratching may cause lichenification.

questions.stem: What is the mainstay of long-term management of atopic eczema in children?

options.label: E
options.text: Daily antifungal treatment for children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Regular liberal use of emollients
questions.initialExplanation: Emollients restore and maintain the skin barrier and should be used regularly, even when the eczema is relatively clear.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Emollients — Correct. They are the foundation of ongoing treatment and help reduce dryness and flares.
- B. No bathing — Incorrect. Gentle washing with soap substitutes/emollients may be used; avoid harsh soaps and irritants.
- C. Systemic steroids — Incorrect. They are not routine maintenance therapy because of adverse effects and rebound risk.
- D. Continuous antibiotics — Incorrect. Antibiotics are reserved for clinically suspected bacterial infection.
- E. Antifungals for all — Incorrect. Fungal treatment is only indicated when there is a relevant fungal infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Emollients are the foundation of eczema care.
- Avoid soap, perfumed products, and known irritants.
- Topical corticosteroid potency should match site, age, and flare severity under clinical guidance.

questions.stem: A child with atopic eczema develops an acute inflammatory flare despite regular emollient use. Which treatment is commonly added for the affected area?

options.label: D
options.text: Long-term systemic antibiotics in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: An appropriately selected topical corticosteroid
questions.initialExplanation: Topical corticosteroids are used for active inflammation, with potency selected according to age, body site, and severity; emollients continue throughout.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Antifungal therapy — Incorrect. It is not routine treatment unless a fungal infection is diagnosed.
- B. Stop emollients — Incorrect. Emollients remain essential for barrier care.

- C. Isotretinoin — Incorrect. This is not a treatment for atopic eczema.
- D. Antibiotics for every flare — Incorrect. Eczema is inflammatory; antibiotics are used only when bacterial infection is suspected/confirmed.
- E. Topical corticosteroid — Correct. It reduces inflammatory activity during a flare when used appropriately.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Emollient: continuous barrier maintenance.
- Topical corticosteroid: short, site-appropriate treatment of inflammation.
- Review adherence, application amount, irritants, and infection when eczema is poorly controlled.

questions.stem: A child with atopic eczema develops rapidly worsening painful monomorphic vesicles and punched-out erosions, with fever. What complication should be suspected?

options.label: C
options.text: Eczema herpeticum due to herpes simplex virus

questions.correctAnswerText: Eczema herpeticum due to herpes simplex virus
questions.initialExplanation: Eczema herpeticum is a potentially serious HSV infection affecting eczematous skin and requires urgent systemic antiviral treatment and same-day specialist advice.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pityriasis rosea — Incorrect. It causes a self-limited scaly macular eruption, often with a herald patch.
- B. Seborrheic dermatitis — Incorrect. It causes greasy scale and is usually not acutely painful or febrile.

- C. Eczema herpeticum — Correct. Rapidly spreading painful monomorphic vesicles/erosions and systemic symptoms in a child with eczema are concerning.
- D. Irritant diaper rash — Incorrect. It is localized to the napkin area and does not cause this vesicular pattern.
- E. Molluscum — Incorrect. It causes discrete umbilicated papules and is usually not acutely febrile.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Suspected eczema herpeticum is urgent.
- Start systemic aciclovir promptly according to local protocol and arrange same-day specialist assessment.
- Consider bacterial co-infection if there is purulence, crusting, or systemic illness.

questions.stem: Which factor may exacerbate atopic eczema?

options.label: A
options.text: Skin irritants such as soap and harsh detergents

questions.correctAnswerText: Skin irritants such as soap and harsh detergents
questions.initialExplanation: Irritants, allergens, heat, infection, stress, and changes in treatment adherence may trigger eczema flares.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Harsh soap/detergents — Correct. They disrupt the skin barrier and can worsen inflammation.
- B. Trigger avoidance — Incorrect. Avoiding known triggers generally helps.
- C. Emollients — Incorrect. These are a cornerstone of treatment, although an individual product may irritate and need changing.
- D. Cotton clothing — Incorrect. Soft breathable clothing may reduce irritation.
- E. Adherence — Incorrect. Appropriate adherence supports control.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Identify individual triggers rather than imposing unnecessary broad restrictions.
- Avoid harsh soap and biological detergents if they trigger symptoms.
- Infection can cause acute worsening.

questions.stem: Which finding most strongly supports irritant diaper dermatitis rather than candidal diaper dermatitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Involvement of folds with satellite pustules

options.label: B
options.text: Erythematous rash over convex surfaces with sparing of skin folds

options.label: C
options.text: Rash spreading into the groin folds with small pustules

options.label: D
options.text: Satellite lesions at the edge of the rash

questions.correctAnswerText: Erythematous rash over convex surfaces with sparing of skin folds
questions.initialExplanation: Irritant diaper dermatitis usually affects exposed convex surfaces and spares the folds; Candida commonly involves folds and satellite lesions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Fold involvement and satellites — Incorrect. This favors candidal dermatitis.
- B. Convex surfaces and fold sparing — Correct. This is the classic irritant pattern.
- C. Fold involvement with pustules — Incorrect. This suggests Candida rather than simple irritant dermatitis.

- D. Satellite lesions — Incorrect. These are characteristic of Candida.
- E. Oral thrush — Incorrect. This may accompany candidal infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Irritant diaper dermatitis: folds usually spared.
- Change diapers frequently; use barrier protection such as zinc oxide.
- Treat diarrhea and keep the area clean and dry.

questions.stem: An infant has a bright erythematous diaper rash involving the skin folds, with satellite pustules. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Candidal diaper dermatitis
questions.initialExplanation: Candida diaper dermatitis typically involves the folds and has satellite papules or pustules; oral thrush may coexist.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Seborrheic dermatitis — Incorrect. This often causes greasy scale on scalp and other seborrheic areas.
- B. Irritant dermatitis — Incorrect. It generally spares skin folds.
- C. Atopic eczema — Incorrect. The napkin area is often relatively spared in classic atopic eczema.
- D. Candida — Correct. Fold involvement and satellite pustules are typical.
- E. Pityriasis rosea — Incorrect. This is a different generalized scaly eruption.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Candida: folds involved, satellite lesions, sometimes oral thrush.
- Treat with an appropriate topical antifungal and reduce moisture/irritation.
- Reassess if persistent or atypical; consider other diagnoses.

questions.stem: A child has multiple small pearly papules with central umbilication. Which organism causes this condition?
questions.correctAnswerText: Poxvirus
questions.initialExplanation: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus and produces characteristic centrally umbilicated papules.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. VZV — Incorrect. It causes chickenpox and shingles.
- B. Poxvirus — Correct. It causes molluscum contagiosum.
- C. HPV — Incorrect. It causes viral warts.
- D. HSV — Incorrect. It causes grouped vesicles and may cause eczema herpeticum.
- E. Sarcoptes — Incorrect. This mite causes scabies.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Molluscum: dome-shaped, pearly, centrally umbilicated papules.
- Often resolves spontaneously.
- Treatment is usually reserved for selected troublesome, painful, spreading, or cosmetically distressing lesions.

questions.stem: Common viral warts on the fingers and toes are caused by:
questions.correctAnswerText: Human papillomavirus
questions.initialExplanation: Common warts are caused by HPV and may resolve spontaneously, especially in children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Candida — Incorrect. This is a yeast that may cause mucocutaneous candidiasis.

- B. HSV — Incorrect. It causes herpes infections.
- C. VZV — Incorrect. It causes varicella and zoster.
- D. Poxvirus — Incorrect. It causes molluscum contagiosum.
- E. HPV — Correct. It causes verrucae/warts.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Viral warts: HPV.
- Many resolve spontaneously.
- Treatment is considered for painful, persistent, spreading, or cosmetically troublesome lesions.

questions.stem: Which organism causes scabies?
questions.correctAnswerText: Sarcoptes scabiei mite
questions.initialExplanation: Scabies is an infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, producing intense itch and characteristic burrows.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Sarcoptes scabiei — Correct. The mite burrows into the epidermis and causes hypersensitivity-related itching.
- B. Poxvirus — Incorrect. This causes molluscum contagiosum.

- C. Candida — Incorrect. This causes fungal infection.
- D. Head louse — Incorrect. This causes pediculosis capitis.
- E. HPV — Incorrect. This causes warts.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Scabies: intense nocturnal itch and burrows.
- Common sites: finger webs, wrists, axillae, waistline, genital area; infants may involve palms, soles, and scalp/trunk.
- Close contacts often itch as well.

questions.stem: Compared with older children, which additional sites are commonly involved in infantile scabies?
questions.correctAnswerText: Palms and soles
questions.initialExplanation: Infants and young children may have a more widespread distribution of scabies, including palms, soles, and trunk.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Face only — Incorrect. The face alone is not the typical distribution.
- B. Elbows only — Incorrect. The distribution is broader.
- C. Nails only — Incorrect. Nail involvement is not the characteristic finding.

- D. Palms and soles — Correct. These sites are commonly involved in infants.
- E. Scalp only — Incorrect. Infantile scabies is not limited to the scalp.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Infant scabies may affect palms, soles, trunk, and sometimes scalp.
- Ask about itchy household contacts.
- Consider scabies when a child has widespread itch, especially at night.

questions.stem: Which management principle is essential when treating scabies in a household?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop treatment as soon as itching begins to improve

options.label: B
options.text: Treat the child with the rash

options.label: C
options.text: Treat close household contacts at the same time according to local guidance

options.label: D
options.text: Use oral antibiotics as the treatment

options.label: E
options.text: Treat if the skin scraping is positive

questions.correctAnswerText: Treat close household contacts at the same time according to local guidance
questions.initialExplanation: Simultaneous treatment of close contacts helps prevent reinfestation; topical scabicides such as permethrin are commonly used according to age and local protocols.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Stop when itch improves — Incorrect. Follow the full treatment instructions; itch may persist after successful eradication.

- B. Child only — Incorrect. This increases the risk of reinfestation.
- C. Treat contacts — Correct. Asymptomatic contacts may still be incubating infestation and can reinfect the child.
- D. Antibiotics only — Incorrect. Antibiotics do not kill the mite.
- E. Scraping required — Incorrect. Diagnosis is often clinical; negative scraping does not exclude scabies.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Treat close contacts simultaneously.
- Use a recommended scabicide appropriate for the child's age.
- Follow instructions for repeat application, clothing, bedding, and contact precautions.
- Persistent itch for a short period after treatment does not necessarily mean treatment failure.

questions.stem: A school-aged child has scalp itching and occipital lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pediculosis capitis
questions.initialExplanation: Head lice commonly cause scalp and nape itching; scratching can lead to secondary bacterial infection and occipital lymphadenopathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pityriasis rosea — Incorrect. This causes a scaly trunk eruption with a herald patch.
- B. Scabies — Incorrect. This typically causes generalized nocturnal itch and burrows at characteristic sites.
- C. Pediculosis capitis — Correct. It is common in school-aged children and is diagnosed by detecting live lice or viable eggs.
- D. Molluscum — Incorrect. This causes umbilicated papules.
- E. Atopic eczema — Incorrect. This causes a chronic itchy inflammatory rash, not live lice.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Head lice: scalp/nape pruritus; inspect for live lice.
- Wet combing with a fine-toothed comb is a safe physical method.
- Follow local guidance for repeat treatment and contact management.

questions.stem: Which feature is characteristic of pityriasis rosea?

options.label: B
options.text: Thick yellow scalp scale in a comfortable infant

options.label: C
options.text: Intense nocturnal itch with burrows between the fingers

options.label: E
options.text: A herald patch followed by smaller lesions in a Christmas-tree pattern on the trunk

questions.correctAnswerText: A herald patch followed by smaller lesions in a Christmas-tree pattern on the trunk
questions.initialExplanation: Pityriasis rosea often begins with a single herald patch followed days later by multiple smaller oval scaly lesions aligned along skin cleavage lines.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Molluscum — Incorrect. This causes centrally umbilicated papules.
- B. Seborrheic dermatitis — Incorrect. This causes greasy scalp scale.
- C. Scabies — Incorrect. This causes nocturnal itch and burrows.
- D. Atopic eczema — Incorrect. This is an itchy eczematous condition.

- E. Herald patch and Christmas-tree distribution — Correct. This is the typical pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Herald patch precedes generalized eruption.
- Trunk lesions may align along cleavage lines ("Christmas-tree" pattern).
- Usually self-limited over several weeks; treatment is often unnecessary unless symptomatic.

questions.stem: A child presents with fever, rapidly spreading petechiae/purpura, and signs of shock. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Meningococcal sepsis
questions.initialExplanation: Fever with a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash and systemic illness is a medical emergency; meningococcal disease and other causes of sepsis must be considered.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Allergic rhinitis — Incorrect. It causes nasal/ocular allergy symptoms, not a purpuric rash with shock.

- B. Seborrheic dermatitis — Incorrect. It causes greasy scale, not purpura and shock.
- C. Molluscum — Incorrect. It causes localized umbilicated papules.
- D. Meningococcal sepsis — Correct. It can progress rapidly and requires emergency assessment and treatment.
- E. Pityriasis rosea — Incorrect. It is a benign scaly eruption without septic shock.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fever plus non-blanching rash: urgent assessment.
- Do not delay emergency management while waiting for rash evolution.
- Consider sepsis, meningococcal disease, DIC, thrombocytopenia, and vasculitis.

questions.stem: Which condition is a classic cause of a vesicular rash in children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Varicella (chickenpox)
questions.initialExplanation: Varicella causes a generalized vesicular eruption, often with lesions in different stages of development.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Roseola — Incorrect. It classically causes fever followed by a maculopapular rash as fever resolves.

- B. Rubella — Incorrect. It causes a maculopapular rash.
- C. Parvovirus B19 — Incorrect. It classically causes slapped-cheek appearance and a lacy rash.
- D. Scarlet fever — Incorrect. It causes a fine sandpaper-like scarlatiniform rash.
- E. Varicella — Correct. It is a classic vesicular viral rash.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Vesicular rash: consider varicella, HSV, enteroviruses, and other causes.
- Fever plus purpura is a different, urgent clinical pattern.
- Immunization status changes the differential but does not eliminate all infections.

## Pediatric Allergy and Anaphylaxis

questions.stem: Which statement best defines an allergic reaction?

options.label: A
options.text: A normal physiological response to exercise

options.label: B
options.text: A hypersensitivity reaction initiated by a specific immunological mechanism

options.label: C
options.text: A reaction caused by bacterial infection

options.label: D
options.text: A genetic condition that typically causes anaphylaxis

options.label: E
options.text: Any non-immune adverse effect after eating food

questions.correctAnswerText: A hypersensitivity reaction initiated by a specific immunological mechanism
questions.initialExplanation: Allergy refers to a hypersensitivity reaction initiated by a specific immune mechanism; it may be IgE-mediated or non-IgE-mediated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Exercise response — Incorrect. This is not a definition of allergy.
- B. Immune-mediated hypersensitivity — Correct. This is the definition used.
- C. Bacterial infection — Incorrect. Infection is not an allergic mechanism.
- D. Always anaphylaxis — Incorrect. Allergic disease ranges from mild local symptoms to severe systemic reactions.

- E. Any adverse food effect — Incorrect. Food intolerance may be non-immune and is not necessarily an allergy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Allergy = immune-mediated hypersensitivity.
- IgE-mediated and non-IgE-mediated mechanisms exist.
- Food intolerance is not the same as food allergy.

questions.stem: What is atopy?

options.label: A
options.text: A bacterial infection of the skin

options.label: C
options.text: An inability to produce any immunoglobulins

options.label: D
options.text: A personal or familial tendency to develop IgE responses to common environmental allergens

options.label: E
options.text: A disorder caused by food poisoning

questions.correctAnswerText: A personal or familial tendency to develop IgE responses to common environmental allergens
questions.initialExplanation: Atopy is a genetic tendency to develop IgE-mediated sensitization and is associated with eczema, allergic rhinitis, and asthma.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Skin infection — Incorrect. Bacterial infection is not atopy.
- B. Anaphylaxis — Incorrect. Anaphylaxis is a severe systemic allergic reaction, not the definition of atopy.
- C. No immunoglobulins — Incorrect. Atopy involves a tendency to produce IgE, not absence of antibodies.

- D. Atopic tendency — Correct. This is the concept described.
- E. Food poisoning — Incorrect. This is not an immune atopic condition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Atopy is associated with eczema, allergic rhinitis, conjunctivitis, and asthma.
- A family history of atopy increases risk.
- Atopy does not mean that anaphylaxis will inevitably occur.

questions.stem: Which sequence best represents the typical allergic march described?

options.label: A
options.text: Food poisoning followed by bacterial sepsis

options.label: B
options.text: Eczema/food allergy in infancy, followed by allergic rhinitis and asthma in later childhood

options.label: C
options.text: Urticaria in infancy followed by renal failure

options.label: D
options.text: Asthma in the neonatal period followed by congenital heart disease

questions.correctAnswerText: Eczema/food allergy in infancy, followed by allergic rhinitis and asthma in later childhood
questions.initialExplanation: The allergic march describes the tendency for atopic manifestations to appear at different ages, although not every child follows the same sequence.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Infection — Incorrect. Food poisoning and sepsis are not allergic diseases.
- B. Typical allergic progression — Correct. Eczema and food allergy may appear early, with rhinitis and asthma developing later in some children.
- C. Renal failure — Incorrect. This is not an atopic progression.
- D. Congenital heart disease — Incorrect. This is unrelated to the allergic march.
- E. Malignancy — Incorrect. Cancer is not part of the allergic march.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- The allergic march is a pattern, not an inevitable sequence.
- Eczema and food allergy may precede rhinitis and asthma.
- Many children do not develop every atopic condition.

questions.stem: Which symptom cluster is typical of allergic rhinitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Productive cough, hemoptysis, and pleuritic chest pain

options.label: B
options.text: Sneezing, nasal itching, congestion, and watery rhinorrhea

options.label: C
options.text: Jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine

options.label: E
options.text: Severe abdominal pain and bilious vomiting

questions.correctAnswerText: Sneezing, nasal itching, congestion, and watery rhinorrhea
questions.initialExplanation: Allergic rhinitis commonly causes nasal itching, sneezing, congestion, and rhinorrhea, often with ocular itching or redness.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Respiratory/lower airway symptoms — Incorrect. These suggest other respiratory conditions.
- B. Allergic rhinitis — Correct. This is the classic symptom pattern.
- C. Cholestasis — Incorrect. These are features of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
- D. Bleeding disorder — Incorrect. Petechiae and mucosal bleeding suggest hematologic or vascular pathology.

- E. Gastrointestinal obstruction — Incorrect. Bilious vomiting is a red flag for obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Allergic rhinitis: sneezing, nasal itch, congestion, watery rhinorrhea.
- Ocular itching and redness may coexist.
- Ask about atopy, seasonality, exposures, and sleep disturbance.

questions.stem: What is an “allergic salute”?

options.label: A
options.text: A circular rash around the mouth

options.label: B
options.text: A transverse crease across the nose caused by repeated upward rubbing

options.label: C
options.text: A line beneath the lower eyelids

options.label: E
options.text: A bluish discoloration around the eyes

questions.correctAnswerText: A transverse crease across the nose caused by repeated upward rubbing
questions.initialExplanation: The allergic salute is the habitual upward rubbing of the nose, which may produce a transverse nasal crease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Perioral rash — Incorrect. This is unrelated.

- B. Nasal crease from rubbing — Correct. This is the allergic salute.
- C. Dennie-Morgan lines — Incorrect. These are infraorbital folds.
- D. Pale turbinates — Incorrect. This may be an examination sign in allergic rhinitis, but it is not the allergic salute.
- E. Allergic shiners — Incorrect. These are bluish infraorbital discoloration.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Allergic salute: transverse nasal crease from rubbing.
- Allergic shiners: infraorbital darkening.
- Dennie-Morgan lines: infraorbital folds.

questions.stem: Which treatment is a mainstay for persistent or moderate-to-severe allergic rhinitis in children?

options.label: D
options.text: Routine systemic corticosteroid for long-term use

questions.correctAnswerText: Intranasal corticosteroid
questions.initialExplanation: Intranasal corticosteroids are highly effective for nasal symptoms, particularly congestion, and are commonly used for persistent allergic rhinitis with age-appropriate products.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Intranasal corticosteroid — Correct. This is an effective first-line option for persistent/moderate-to-severe symptoms.
- B. Long-term decongestant — Incorrect. Prolonged topical decongestant use can cause rhinitis medicamentosa.
- C. Antibiotics — Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis is not a bacterial infection.
- D. Long-term systemic steroid — Incorrect. Systemic corticosteroids are generally avoided for routine rhinitis because of adverse effects.
- E. Antifungal — Incorrect. Fungi are not the usual cause of allergic rhinitis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Intranasal corticosteroids are important for persistent symptoms.
- Non-sedating antihistamines help sneezing/itching.
- Avoid prolonged topical decongestant use because of rebound congestion.
- Allergen avoidance and correct spray technique improve control.

questions.stem: Which lesion defines urticaria?
questions.correctAnswerText: Transient raised wheal
questions.initialExplanation: Urticaria is characterized by transient wheals, often itchy, caused by dermal edema from mast-cell mediator release.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Wheal — Correct. Wheals are raised, often blanching lesions that usually resolve within 24 hours at an individual site.
- B. Umbilicated papule — Incorrect. This is typical of molluscum contagiosum.
- C. Ulcer — Incorrect. This is not the defining lesion of urticaria.

- D. Greasy scale — Incorrect. This suggests seborrheic dermatitis.
- E. Honey crust — Incorrect. This suggests impetigo.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Urticaria = transient itchy wheals.
- Angioedema may involve deeper tissues.
- Assess for anaphylaxis if respiratory, cardiovascular, or significant gastrointestinal symptoms accompany skin findings.

questions.stem: Papular urticaria in children is commonly a hypersensitivity reaction to:

options.label: A
options.text: Insect bites such as fleas or mites

questions.correctAnswerText: Insect bites such as fleas or mites
questions.initialExplanation: Papular urticaria is a recurrent hypersensitivity response to insect bites, often affecting exposed areas such as the legs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Insect bites — Correct. Fleas, mites, and other arthropods may trigger the eruption.
- B. Vitamin D deficiency — Incorrect. This causes rickets, not papular urticaria.
- C. Streptococcal toxins — Incorrect. These cause other infectious syndromes.
- D. Hepatitis viruses — Incorrect. These cause liver infection, not papular urticaria.
- E. Autoimmune hemolysis — Incorrect. This is unrelated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Papular urticaria often affects the legs and exposed skin.
- Lesions may recur after repeated bites.
- Investigate environmental exposure and household pets when relevant.

questions.stem: Which presentation most strongly suggests anaphylaxis?

options.label: A
options.text: Sudden onset of airway, breathing, or circulation compromise after a likely allergen exposure, often with skin or mucosal changes

options.label: B
options.text: A stable papular rash following insect bites

options.label: C
options.text: Long-standing dry skin without systemic symptoms

options.label: D
options.text: A single localized itchy wheal with normal breathing and circulation

options.label: E
options.text: Isolated chronic nasal congestion for 6 months

questions.correctAnswerText: Sudden onset of airway, breathing, or circulation compromise after a likely allergen exposure, often with skin or mucosal changes
questions.initialExplanation: Anaphylaxis is a rapid-onset, potentially life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction involving airway, breathing, or circulation compromise.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Acute systemic compromise — Correct. This is the key clinical pattern; skin signs are common but may be absent.
- B. Papular bite reaction — Incorrect. This is a localized delayed hypersensitivity pattern.

- C. Dry skin — Incorrect. This is not an acute systemic reaction.
- D. Isolated wheal — Incorrect. Localized urticaria without systemic involvement is not anaphylaxis.
- E. Chronic rhinitis — Incorrect. This is not anaphylaxis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis.
- Look for acute airway, breathing, or circulation problems after exposure.
- Skin manifestations may be absent; do not wait for a rash before treating a convincing reaction.

questions.stem: What is the first-line medication for acute anaphylaxis in a child?

options.label: D
options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) into the anterolateral thigh

questions.correctAnswerText: Intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) into the anterolateral thigh
questions.initialExplanation: IM adrenaline is the first-line treatment and should be administered promptly; antihistamines and corticosteroids must not delay it.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Salbutamol — Incorrect. It may help persistent bronchospasm as an adjunct but does not replace adrenaline.
- B. Oral antihistamine — Incorrect. It may help skin symptoms but does not treat life-threatening airway or circulatory compromise.
- C. Antibiotic — Incorrect. Anaphylaxis is not a bacterial infection.

- D. IM adrenaline — Correct. It treats airway edema, bronchospasm, and circulatory compromise.
- E. IV hydrocortisone — Incorrect. Steroids have a delayed effect and are not first-line resuscitation treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- IM adrenaline first, anterolateral thigh.
- Repeat according to the emergency protocol if there is no adequate response.
- Do not delay adrenaline for antihistamines, steroids, IV access, or investigations.

questions.stem: What is an appropriate immediate supportive action for a child with suspected anaphylaxis?

options.label: A
options.text: Give oral fluids and observe without monitoring

options.label: B
options.text: Call for help, assess ABCDE, and keep the child lying flat with legs elevated if tolerated

options.label: C
options.text: Delay treatment until skin testing is completed

options.label: D
options.text: Sit each patient upright regardless of circulatory status

options.label: E
options.text: Make the child stand and walk

questions.correctAnswerText: Call for help, assess ABCDE, and keep the child lying flat with legs elevated if tolerated
questions.initialExplanation: Early help, ABCDE assessment, appropriate positioning, IM adrenaline, oxygen/monitoring, and fluid resuscitation when indicated are core emergency actions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Oral fluids only — Incorrect. This is inadequate for anaphylaxis.
- B. Immediate supportive management — Correct. Lying flat helps avoid sudden circulatory collapse; position may be adjusted if breathing is difficult.
- C. Allergy testing first — Incorrect. Emergency treatment must not be delayed.
- D. Upright for everyone — Incorrect. Position should be individualized; a patient with circulatory compromise should generally not be stood or sat upright suddenly.

- E. Walking — Incorrect. Standing or walking can worsen circulatory compromise.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Call emergency assistance.
- ABCDE and IM adrenaline are priorities.
- Oxygen, monitoring, and IV crystalloid are used as indicated.
- Do not allow a shocked patient to stand or walk.

questions.stem: A child with anaphylaxis continues to wheeze after receiving appropriate IM adrenaline. Which intervention may be added while continuing emergency management?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop adrenaline and give an oral antihistamine

options.label: B
options.text: Inhaled/nebulized beta-2 agonist for persistent bronchospasm

options.label: C
options.text: Give an antibiotic as the next essential treatment

options.label: D
options.text: Delay most further treatment until serum IgE returns

questions.correctAnswerText: Inhaled/nebulized beta-2 agonist for persistent bronchospasm
questions.initialExplanation: Inhaled bronchodilators may be used as adjuncts for persistent wheeze, but they do not replace repeat IM adrenaline when anaphylaxis remains unresolved.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Stop adrenaline — Incorrect. Antihistamines do not treat airway or circulatory compromise and should not replace adrenaline.
- B. Inhaled beta-2 agonist — Correct. It can improve bronchospasm while the primary anaphylaxis algorithm continues.
- C. Antibiotic — Incorrect. This is not anaphylaxis treatment.
- D. Wait for IgE — Incorrect. Treatment is clinical and time-critical.
- E. Emollient — Incorrect. This has no role in acute systemic anaphylaxis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Adrenaline remains first-line.
- Bronchodilator is an adjunct for persistent bronchospasm.
- Antihistamines are for selected skin symptoms after initial stabilization, not for airway/circulatory compromise.
- Steroids are not a substitute for adrenaline and are not routinely relied on for acute resuscitation.

## Viral Hepatitis and Acute Liver Failure

topics.name: Viral Hepatitis and Acute Liver Failure

questions.stem: Which hepatitis virus is a DNA virus, unlike the other major hepatitis viruses discussed?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hepatitis B virus
questions.initialExplanation: HBV is a partially double-stranded DNA virus; HAV, HCV, HDV, and HEV are RNA viruses.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. HAV — Incorrect. HAV is an RNA virus.
- B. HBV — Correct. Hepatitis B is the DNA virus in this group.
- C. HDV — Incorrect. HDV is an RNA virus and requires HBV surface antigen to complete its life cycle.
- D. HCV — Incorrect. HCV is an RNA virus.
- E. HEV — Incorrect. HEV is an RNA virus.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HBV: DNA virus.
- HAV, HCV, HDV, HEV: RNA viruses.
- HDV depends on HBV; hepatitis B vaccination prevents hepatitis D infection.

questions.stem: Which pair of hepatitis viruses is mainly transmitted by the fecal-oral route?
questions.correctAnswerText: HAV and HEV
questions.initialExplanation: HAV and HEV are primarily transmitted by the fecal-oral route, often through contaminated food or water.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. HBV and HCV — Incorrect. These are mainly transmitted through blood and, for HBV, also sexual and perinatal routes.
- B. HCV and HDV — Incorrect. These are not fecal-oral viruses.
- C. HBV and HDV — Incorrect. These are transmitted through blood/body fluids; HDV requires HBV.
- D. HBV and HGV — Incorrect. This is not the fecal-oral pair.

- E. HAV and HEV — Correct. These are the classic fecal-oral hepatitis viruses.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HAV/HEV: fecal-oral.
- HBV/HCV/HDV: principally blood/body-fluid transmission.
- Improve sanitation and food/water safety to reduce enterically transmitted hepatitis.

questions.stem: Which statement about hepatitis D virus is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is an independent DNA virus

options.label: B
options.text: It requires hepatitis B surface antigen to form infectious particles

options.label: C
options.text: It infects in the absence of HBV

options.label: D
options.text: It is prevented by a separate routinely used HDV vaccine

options.label: E
options.text: It is transmitted by contaminated food

questions.correctAnswerText: It requires hepatitis B surface antigen to form infectious particles
questions.initialExplanation: HDV is a defective RNA virus that depends on HBV surface antigen; preventing HBV infection also prevents HDV infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Independent DNA virus — Incorrect. HDV is an RNA virus and is not independent of HBV.
- B. Requires HBsAg — Correct. HDV depends on HBV for assembly and propagation.
- C. Absence of HBV — Incorrect. HDV cannot establish productive infection without HBV.
- D. Separate routine vaccine — Incorrect. Prevention is through hepatitis B vaccination.
- E. Contaminated food only — Incorrect. HDV is transmitted through blood/body fluids, not the fecal-oral route.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HDV requires HBV.
- HBV vaccination prevents HDV infection.
- Coinfection or superinfection can cause severe hepatitis.

questions.stem: Which serological marker indicates acute or recent hepatitis A infection?
questions.correctAnswerText: Anti-HAV IgM
questions.initialExplanation: Anti-HAV IgM supports acute or recent hepatitis A infection; HAV does not cause a chronic carrier state.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Anti-HBc IgG — Incorrect. This indicates previous exposure to HBV or chronic infection depending on the full serological pattern.
- B. Anti-HAV IgM — Correct. It is the key serological marker for acute/recent HAV infection.
- C. HBsAg — Incorrect. This indicates current hepatitis B infection.
- D. Anti-HBs — Incorrect. This indicates immunity due to vaccination or recovery, depending on anti-HBc.

- E. Anti-HCV alone — Incorrect. It indicates exposure and requires HCV RNA testing to confirm current infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HAV: anti-HAV IgM for acute infection.
- HAV does not cause chronic infection or a chronic carrier state.
- Management is usually supportive; monitor for rare acute liver failure.

questions.stem: A newborn is delivered by a mother who is HBsAg-positive. What should the infant receive promptly after birth?

options.label: A
options.text: No prophylaxis if the infant appears well

options.label: D
options.text: Hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG in separate injection sites within 12 hours

questions.correctAnswerText: Hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG in separate injection sites within 12 hours
questions.initialExplanation: Infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers require prompt active and passive immunoprophylaxis to reduce perinatal HBV transmission.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. No prophylaxis — Incorrect. The infant may be asymptomatic while remaining at high risk of infection.
- B. HCV immunoglobulin — Incorrect. There is no equivalent standard HCV immunoglobulin prophylaxis.
- C. Antiviral only — Incorrect. It does not replace newborn vaccine and HBIG prophylaxis.
- D. Vaccine plus HBIG — Correct. Both should be administered promptly, ideally within 12 hours, in separate limbs/sites.
- E. Hepatitis A vaccine — Incorrect. It does not prevent perinatal HBV infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HBsAg-positive mother: HBV vaccine + HBIG promptly after birth.
- Complete the vaccine series and arrange post-vaccination serological testing according to local guidance.
- Do not delay prophylaxis while waiting for newborn symptoms.

questions.stem: Which serological pattern is most consistent with acute hepatitis B infection?

options.label: B
options.text: HBsAg negative, anti-HBc negative, anti-HBs negative

options.label: C
options.text: HBsAg positive and anti-HBc IgM positive

options.label: D
options.text: Anti-HBs positive with anti-HBc negative after vaccination

options.label: E
options.text: Anti-HBc IgG positive and anti-HBs positive, with HBsAg negative

questions.correctAnswerText: HBsAg positive and anti-HBc IgM positive
questions.initialExplanation: HBsAg indicates current infection, while anti-HBc IgM is a key marker of acute or recent HBV infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Anti-HBs alone — Incorrect. This commonly indicates immunity after vaccination.
- B. All negative — Incorrect. This indicates susceptibility if the person has not been vaccinated.
- C. HBsAg plus anti-HBc IgM — Correct. This is the typical acute infection pattern.
- D. Anti-HBs with anti-HBc negative — Incorrect. This is the usual pattern after vaccination, not acute infection.

- E. Anti-HBc IgG plus anti-HBs — Incorrect. With HBsAg negative, this usually indicates resolved natural infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HBsAg: current HBV infection.
- Anti-HBc IgM: acute/recent infection.
- Anti-HBs: immunity.
- Interpret the complete panel rather than a single marker.

questions.stem: Which serological pattern is typical after successful hepatitis B vaccination?

options.label: A
options.text: HBsAg positive with anti-HBc IgM positive

options.label: B
options.text: HBsAg positive with anti-HBc IgG positive

options.label: D
options.text: Anti-HBc IgG positive with anti-HBs negative

questions.correctAnswerText: Anti-HBs positive with anti-HBc negative
questions.initialExplanation: Hepatitis B vaccination produces anti-HBs without anti-HBc because the vaccine contains surface antigen, not core antigen.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Acute infection — Incorrect. HBsAg and anti-HBc IgM indicate acute infection.
- B. Chronic infection — Incorrect. HBsAg and anti-HBc IgG suggest chronic infection.
- C. Anti-HBs only — Correct. This is the expected vaccine-induced immunity pattern.
- D. Isolated core antibody — Incorrect. This requires further interpretation and is not the typical vaccine pattern.
- E. All markers — Incorrect. This is not the usual post-vaccination pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Vaccinated: anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc negative.
- Resolved natural infection: anti-HBc IgG and anti-HBs positive, HBsAg negative.
- Acute infection: HBsAg and anti-HBc IgM positive.

questions.stem: What is an important route of hepatitis C transmission in children?

options.label: A
options.text: Vertical transmission from an infected mother

options.label: C
options.text: Fecal-oral spread through contaminated water as the main route

options.label: E
options.text: Sharing food utensils in ordinary household contact

questions.correctAnswerText: Vertical transmission from an infected mother
questions.initialExplanation: Vertical transmission is an important route of HCV infection in children; blood exposure is also a major transmission route.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Vertical transmission — Correct. Perinatal transmission is a major route in pediatric HCV.
- B. Casual school contact — Incorrect. HCV is not spread by routine casual contact.
- C. Fecal-oral — Incorrect. This is typical of HAV and HEV.
- D. Mosquitoes — Incorrect. HCV is not transmitted by mosquito bites.
- E. Shared utensils — Incorrect. Ordinary household sharing does not transmit HCV.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pediatric HCV: vertical transmission is important.
- HCV is primarily blood-borne.
- Assess maternal infection and follow pediatric testing pathways for exposed infants.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects current treatment of chronic hepatitis C in children?

options.label: A
options.text: Interferon and ribavirin are the available treatments for most children

options.label: C
options.text: Hepatitis B vaccine treats established HCV infection

options.label: D
options.text: No child should be treated before adulthood

options.label: E
options.text: Approved direct-acting antiviral regimens are recommended for eligible children aged 3 years and older

questions.correctAnswerText: Approved direct-acting antiviral regimens are recommended for eligible children aged 3 years and older
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance's older interferon/ribavirin regimen has been superseded by highly effective oral direct-acting antivirals for children aged 3 years and older, subject to specialist assessment and approved regimens.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Interferon/ribavirin only — Incorrect. These are older regimens and are no longer the standard preferred approach.
- B. Antibiotics — Incorrect. HCV is a virus.
- C. HBV vaccine — Incorrect. It prevents hepatitis B, not established hepatitis C infection.

- D. Wait until adulthood — Incorrect. Eligible children can receive treatment from age 3 years.
- E. Direct-acting antivirals — Correct. Current guidance recommends approved DAA therapy for eligible children aged 3 years and older.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HCV treatment has shifted from interferon-based therapy to direct-acting antivirals.
- Eligible children aged 3 years and older can be treated.
- Check for HBV infection before starting HCV DAA therapy because HBV reactivation can occur.
