questions.stem: Which clinical combination is compatible with acute viral hepatitis in a child?

options.label: B
options.text: Acute unilateral weakness without systemic symptoms

options.label: D
options.text: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, lethargy, jaundice, and tender hepatomegaly

questions.correctAnswerText: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, lethargy, jaundice, and tender hepatomegaly
questions.initialExplanation: Acute hepatitis may cause nonspecific gastrointestinal symptoms, lethargy, jaundice, hepatomegaly, and elevated aminotransferases; many children can be asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Diabetes insipidus — Incorrect. Polyuria and polydipsia alone do not suggest acute hepatitis.

- B. Neurological event — Incorrect. This is not a typical acute hepatitis presentation.
- C. Croup — Incorrect. Stridor and barking cough suggest upper-airway disease.
- D. Acute hepatitis picture — Correct. These are compatible clinical findings.
- E. Urinary tract pathology — Incorrect. Hematuria is not a typical hepatitis presentation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Children may have mild or asymptomatic hepatitis.
- Jaundice may be absent.
- Markedly raised ALT/AST support hepatocellular injury but do not alone determine liver function.

questions.stem: Which combination is most concerning for acute liver failure in a child with acute hepatitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Mild isolated pruritus with normal coagulation

options.label: B
options.text: A single episode of vomiting with normal examination

options.label: D
options.text: Coagulopathy with encephalopathy, hypoglycemia, or worsening consciousness

questions.correctAnswerText: Coagulopathy with encephalopathy, hypoglycemia, or worsening consciousness
questions.initialExplanation: Acute liver failure involves impaired hepatic synthetic function and may be accompanied by encephalopathy, hypoglycemia, and metabolic disturbances; it requires urgent specialist care.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Mild pruritus only — Incorrect. This may occur in cholestasis but does not establish acute liver failure.
- B. One vomit — Incorrect. This is nonspecific without evidence of liver dysfunction.
- C. Mild eczema — Incorrect. This is unrelated to liver failure.

- D. Liver failure features — Correct. Coagulopathy and encephalopathy are major warning signs; hypoglycemia may occur.
- E. Rhinorrhea — Incorrect. This is an upper respiratory symptom.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Monitor PT/INR, glucose, mental status, ammonia, electrolytes, and acid-base status.
- Worsening encephalopathy or coagulopathy is a poor prognostic sign.
- Early referral to a pediatric liver/transplant center is essential.

questions.stem: Which laboratory test is particularly important for assessing hepatic synthetic function in a child with suspected acute liver failure?
questions.correctAnswerText: Prothrombin time/INR
questions.initialExplanation: PT/INR reflects hepatic synthesis of clotting factors and is central to assessing severity of acute liver dysfunction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Urine ketones — Incorrect. These do not assess hepatic synthetic function.
- B. Eosinophils — Incorrect. This is not a liver synthetic marker.

- C. PT/INR — Correct. Prolongation indicates impaired clotting factor synthesis and is important in acute liver failure assessment.
- D. Amylase — Incorrect. This is primarily used in assessment of pancreatic injury.
- E. Sodium — Incorrect. Electrolytes are important but sodium alone does not measure hepatic synthesis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- ALT/AST indicate hepatocellular injury.
- PT/INR assesses synthetic function and severity.
- A worsening INR despite vitamin K correction requires urgent specialist evaluation.

questions.stem: Which finding suggests worsening prognosis in pediatric acute liver failure?

options.label: B
options.text: Improving mental status and normalizing INR

options.label: D
options.text: Resolution of jaundice with stable liver function

questions.correctAnswerText: Worsening encephalopathy with rising INR
questions.initialExplanation: Worsening encephalopathy and progressive coagulopathy are major signs of deterioration and should prompt urgent specialist/transplant-center assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Appetite alone — Incorrect. It does not outweigh objective measures of liver function.
- B. Improvement — Incorrect. These findings suggest recovery rather than deterioration.
- C. Worsening encephalopathy and INR — Correct. These indicate declining hepatic function.
- D. Jaundice resolution — Incorrect. This may be reassuring only when other markers and clinical status improve; it is not enough alone.

- E. Stable glucose and improving coagulation — Incorrect. This is more reassuring.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Follow mental status, PT/INR, glucose, ammonia, bilirubin, lactate, and renal function.
- Clinical deterioration can occur despite changes in aminotransferases.
- Do not delay transplant-center discussion in a deteriorating child.

questions.stem: What is the usual management of uncomplicated acute hepatitis A in children?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate liver transplantation in typical presentations

options.label: B
options.text: Interferon for children in routine care

options.label: E
options.text: Prolonged strict bed rest and a special restrictive diet for children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Supportive care and monitoring
questions.initialExplanation: Most children with acute hepatitis A recover spontaneously; management is supportive, with monitoring for complications and rare acute liver failure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Transplantation for all — Incorrect. Liver transplantation is considered only in selected severe acute liver failure cases.
- B. Interferon — Incorrect. This is not indicated for uncomplicated HAV.
- C. Supportive care — Correct. Maintain hydration and nutrition and monitor clinical status.
- D. Long-term antivirals — Incorrect. There is no routine chronic antiviral treatment for HAV.
- E. Strict bed rest/restrictive diet — Incorrect. Routine strict bed rest or special diet has no established benefit for uncomplicated HAV.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HAV is usually self-limited.
- No chronic carrier state.
- Vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis are important preventive measures according to local guidance.

## Chronic Liver Disease and Specific Hepatic Disorders

topics.name: Chronic Liver Disease and Specific Hepatic Disorders

questions.stem: Which combination is most suggestive of portal hypertension in a child with chronic liver disease?
questions.correctAnswerText: Splenomegaly, ascites, and esophageal varices
questions.initialExplanation: Portal hypertension increases pressure in the portal venous system and may cause splenomegaly, ascites, and portosystemic collaterals including esophageal varices.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Portal hypertension features — Correct. These are classic complications.
- B. Developmental milestones — Incorrect. These are unrelated to portal hypertension.
- C. Beckwith-Wiedemann features — Incorrect. These suggest an overgrowth syndrome.
- D. Urticaria — Incorrect. Wheals are a cutaneous allergic manifestation.

- E. Allergic rhinitis — Incorrect. These are upper-airway allergy symptoms.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Portal hypertension: splenomegaly, ascites, varices, hypersplenism.
- Esophageal varices may present with upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
- Children with chronic liver disease require specialist surveillance.

questions.stem: A child with known portal hypertension presents with hematemesis. Which complication should be suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bleeding esophageal varices
questions.initialExplanation: Portal hypertension can produce esophageal varices, which may rupture and cause life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Otitis media — Incorrect. This is an ear infection.
- B. Allergic rhinitis — Incorrect. This does not cause hematemesis.
- C. Variceal bleeding — Correct. Hematemesis in a child with portal hypertension is an emergency.
- D. Pityriasis rosea — Incorrect. This is a benign skin eruption.

- E. Diaper dermatitis — Incorrect. This is a skin condition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Varices are caused by portal-systemic collateral formation.
- Acute bleeding requires stabilization and urgent specialist/endoscopic management.
- Endoscopy is used for diagnosis and treatment planning.

questions.stem: Which mechanism contributes to ascites in advanced liver disease?

options.label: B
options.text: Increased serum albumin and reduced portal pressure

options.label: C
options.text: Portal hypertension, reduced albumin, and renal sodium/water retention

questions.correctAnswerText: Portal hypertension, reduced albumin, and renal sodium/water retention
questions.initialExplanation: Ascites in chronic liver disease is multifactorial, involving portal hypertension, reduced oncotic pressure, and sodium/water retention related to circulatory and renal changes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Vitamin C deficiency — Incorrect. This causes scurvy, not the main mechanism of cirrhotic ascites.
- B. High albumin and low portal pressure — Incorrect. These would oppose ascites formation.
- C. Portal pressure and sodium retention — Correct. These mechanisms contribute to fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity.
- D. Lymphocytes — Incorrect. This does not explain cirrhotic ascites.

- E. Thyroid hormone alone — Incorrect. This is not the mechanism described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ascites: portal hypertension, low albumin, sodium retention.
- Assess renal function and infection.
- New or worsening ascites in a child with liver disease requires evaluation.

questions.stem: A child with chronic liver disease and ascites develops fever and abdominal tenderness. Which complication should be considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
questions.initialExplanation: Fever, abdominal pain, and tenderness in a child with ascites may indicate spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), which requires urgent diagnostic paracentesis and antimicrobial treatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pityriasis rosea — Incorrect. This is a skin eruption.
- B. Molluscum — Incorrect. This causes umbilicated papules.

- C. Allergic conjunctivitis — Incorrect. This causes itchy/red eyes.
- D. Head lice — Incorrect. This causes scalp itching.
- E. SBP — Correct. Infection of ascitic fluid may cause fever, pain, and tenderness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- SBP: fever and abdominal pain/tenderness in a patient with ascites.
- Diagnostic paracentesis is essential.
- Start appropriate antibiotics promptly according to local pediatric protocols.

questions.stem: A term infant remains jaundiced beyond 14 days. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Ignore pale stools if the infant is feeding

options.label: C
options.text: Stop breastfeeding immediately in each case

options.label: D
options.text: Reassure that most jaundice beyond 2 weeks is physiological

options.label: E
options.text: Investigate prolonged jaundice, including fractionated bilirubin and assessment for conjugated hyperbilirubinemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Investigate prolonged jaundice, including fractionated bilirubin and assessment for conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
questions.initialExplanation: Jaundice persisting beyond 14 days in a term infant requires assessment; conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is always pathological and requires prompt investigation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Ignore pale stools — Incorrect. Pale/acholic stools are a major red flag for cholestasis and biliary obstruction.

- B. Antibiotics without evaluation — Incorrect. Treatment depends on the cause and clinical findings.
- C. Stop breastfeeding — Incorrect. Breastfeeding should not be stopped routinely; the cause must be assessed.
- D. Always physiological — Incorrect. Persistent jaundice may reflect infection, hemolysis, hypothyroidism, or cholestatic disease.
- E. Investigate and fractionate bilirubin — Correct. This distinguishes unconjugated from conjugated causes and helps identify cholestasis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prolonged jaundice: beyond 14 days in term infants; timing differs in preterm infants.
- Measure total and direct/conjugated bilirubin.
- Pale stools and dark urine require urgent evaluation for cholestasis/biliary atresia.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cause of conjugated (cholestatic) neonatal jaundice?
questions.correctAnswerText: Biliary atresia
questions.initialExplanation: Biliary atresia causes extrahepatic biliary obstruction and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia; it is time-critical because early specialist assessment and treatment improve outcomes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Gilbert syndrome — Incorrect. This causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
- B. Physiological jaundice — Incorrect. This is predominantly unconjugated.
- C. Crigler-Najjar — Incorrect. This causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to impaired bilirubin conjugation.

- D. Biliary atresia — Correct. This is a major cause of neonatal cholestasis.
- E. Breast-milk jaundice — Incorrect. This is typically unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Conjugated jaundice is never physiological.
- Biliary atresia: pale stools, dark urine, hepatomegaly, conjugated bilirubin.
- Urgent specialist referral is required; do not wait for spontaneous resolution.

questions.stem: Wilson disease is caused by impaired biliary excretion of which mineral?
questions.correctAnswerText: Copper
questions.initialExplanation: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism, usually due to ATP7B dysfunction, causing copper accumulation in the liver, brain, and other tissues.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Magnesium — Incorrect. Magnesium is not the accumulated metal in Wilson disease.

- B. Copper — Correct. Defective biliary excretion leads to tissue copper accumulation.
- C. Calcium — Incorrect. Calcium disorders cause different clinical syndromes.
- D. Iron — Incorrect. Iron overload is associated with other disorders such as hemochromatosis.
- E. Zinc — Incorrect. Zinc may be used therapeutically to reduce intestinal copper absorption.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Wilson disease: autosomal recessive ATP7B disorder.
- Copper accumulates in liver, brain, kidney, and cornea.
- Can present with liver disease in childhood and neuropsychiatric manifestations later.

questions.stem: Which biochemical finding supports Wilson disease?

options.label: C
options.text: Low urinary copper with normal liver tests

options.label: D
options.text: High serum ceruloplasmin with low urinary copper in each case

options.label: E
options.text: Low serum ceruloplasmin with increased urinary copper

questions.correctAnswerText: Low serum ceruloplasmin with increased urinary copper
questions.initialExplanation: Wilson disease commonly produces low ceruloplasmin and increased urinary copper; no single test should be interpreted in isolation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. High calcium — Incorrect. This is unrelated.
- B. Ferritin alone — Incorrect. Ferritin is not diagnostic of Wilson disease.

- C. Low urinary copper — Incorrect. Untreated symptomatic Wilson disease commonly has increased urinary copper.
- D. High ceruloplasmin/low urine copper — Incorrect. This is not the typical pattern.
- E. Low ceruloplasmin/high urine copper — Correct. This combination supports the diagnosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Investigations include ceruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper, liver tests, slit-lamp examination, and genetic testing.
- Kayser-Fleischer rings may be absent in young children or predominantly hepatic presentations.
- Specialist interpretation is required.

questions.stem: Which treatment reduces copper burden in Wilson disease?

options.label: D
options.text: Copper chelation with agents such as penicillamine or trientine, or zinc in selected cases

questions.correctAnswerText: Copper chelation with agents such as penicillamine or trientine, or zinc in selected cases
questions.initialExplanation: Treatment aims to reduce body copper using chelating agents or zinc to reduce intestinal copper absorption; acute liver failure or severe end-stage disease may require transplantation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Iron — Incorrect. Iron does not remove copper.
- B. Vitamin C alone — Incorrect. This does not treat copper overload.

- C. Copper supplementation — Incorrect. This would worsen accumulation.
- D. Chelation/zinc — Correct. These are established approaches under specialist monitoring.
- E. Antibiotics — Incorrect. Wilson disease is genetic, not bacterial.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Penicillamine/trientine: promote urinary copper excretion.
- Zinc: reduces intestinal copper absorption.
- Monitor for treatment toxicity and adherence.
- Consider liver transplant in acute liver failure or severe end-stage disease.

questions.stem: Which laboratory pattern supports autoimmune hepatitis in a child?

options.label: B
options.text: Low ALT and normal liver function in each case

options.label: D
options.text: Low IgG with isolated elevated serum sodium

options.label: E
options.text: Elevated IgG with positive autoantibodies and compatible liver histology

questions.correctAnswerText: Elevated IgG with positive autoantibodies and compatible liver histology
questions.initialExplanation: Autoimmune hepatitis is supported by raised aminotransferases, hypergammaglobulinemia (particularly IgG), relevant autoantibodies, and compatible histology after excluding other causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Anti-HAV IgM — Incorrect. This indicates acute hepatitis A infection.

- B. Normal ALT — Incorrect. Active autoimmune hepatitis generally causes biochemical evidence of liver injury.
- C. Anti-HBs — Incorrect. This indicates hepatitis B immunity, not autoimmune liver disease.
- D. Low IgG and sodium — Incorrect. This does not support autoimmune hepatitis.
- E. High IgG/autoantibodies/histology — Correct. These are important diagnostic features.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Autoimmune hepatitis can present as acute hepatitis, chronic liver disease, or acute liver failure.
- Treatment commonly involves immunosuppression under specialist care.
- Screen for associated autoimmune disorders when clinically appropriate.

questions.stem: Which condition is a recognized cause of chronic liver disease in older children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Wilson disease
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic pediatric liver disease may result from Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, chronic viral hepatitis, cystic fibrosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and other metabolic or cholestatic conditions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Wilson disease — Correct. It can cause chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and portal hypertension.
- B. Head lice — Incorrect. This is a superficial parasitic infestation.
- C. Molluscum — Incorrect. This is a benign viral skin infection.
- D. Rhinovirus — Incorrect. This usually causes an acute respiratory infection.
- E. Seborrheic dermatitis — Incorrect. This is an inflammatory skin condition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chronic liver disease differential: viral, autoimmune, metabolic/genetic, drug-induced, and cholestatic causes.
- Look for growth failure, pruritus, jaundice, splenomegaly, ascites, and signs of portal hypertension.
- Investigations should be targeted to age and phenotype.

## Pediatric Tumors and Red-Flag Presentations

questions.stem: Which is a common primary malignant liver tumor in young children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hepatoblastoma
questions.initialExplanation: Hepatoblastoma is the most common primary malignant liver tumor in young children and may present with an abdominal mass.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hepatoblastoma — Correct. It is the main malignant hepatic tumor in early childhood.
- B. Hemangioma — Incorrect. This is a vascular tumor, usually benign.
- C. Hepatic adenoma — Incorrect. This is generally benign and less typical in young children.
- D. Cholangiocarcinoma — Incorrect. This is a biliary tract malignancy and is rare in children.
- E. Focal nodular hyperplasia — Incorrect. This is a benign liver lesion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hepatoblastoma: young child, abdominal mass, elevated AFP in many cases.
- Associations include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis.
- Workup and treatment are coordinated by a pediatric oncology/liver tumor team.

questions.stem: Which serum tumor marker is commonly elevated in hepatoblastoma and used for diagnosis/monitoring?
questions.correctAnswerText: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
questions.initialExplanation: AFP is commonly elevated in hepatoblastoma and can be used to monitor response and recurrence, interpreted with age-specific reference ranges.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Thyroglobulin — Incorrect. This is used in selected thyroid conditions and cancers.

- B. Amylase — Incorrect. This is associated with pancreatic injury.
- C. Troponin — Incorrect. This is a marker of myocardial injury.
- D. CA-125 — Incorrect. This is not the standard hepatoblastoma marker.
- E. AFP — Correct. It is an important marker in hepatoblastoma.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- AFP is useful for hepatoblastoma diagnosis/monitoring.
- AFP is physiologically high in newborns; interpret according to age.
- Imaging and histopathology are important parts of definitive diagnosis and staging.

questions.stem: Which background condition increases the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in an adolescent?

options.label: A
options.text: Chronic hepatitis B or C infection

questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic hepatitis B or C infection
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic viral hepatitis can lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; HCC may occur in adolescents with chronic liver disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Chronic HBV/HCV — Correct. These are recognized risk factors for HCC.
- B. Head lice — Incorrect. This is unrelated to hepatic malignancy.

- C. Atopic eczema — Incorrect. This is an inflammatory skin disorder.
- D. Molluscum — Incorrect. This is a benign skin infection.
- E. Scabies — Incorrect. This is a parasitic skin infestation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- HCC may arise in chronic viral hepatitis and chronic liver disease.
- Evaluate unexplained weight loss, abdominal mass, hepatomegaly, and worsening liver function.
- Pediatric HCC management requires specialist staging and multidisciplinary care.

questions.stem: What is the classic presenting sign of retinoblastoma?

options.label: E
options.text: Painful red eye with purulent discharge

questions.correctAnswerText: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex)
questions.initialExplanation: Retinoblastoma is a malignant retinal tumor in childhood; leukocoria is a key warning sign and requires urgent ophthalmological assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Cataracts in every case — Incorrect. Cataract is an important differential diagnosis of leukocoria but is not the universal presentation of retinoblastoma.
- B. Normal red reflex — Incorrect. This is reassuring when symmetric and normal, though it does not exclude every ocular disorder.
- C. Rhinorrhea — Incorrect. This is unrelated.
- D. Leukocoria — Correct. A white pupillary reflex is a classic presentation.
- E. Purulent red eye — Incorrect. This suggests conjunctivitis or another ocular infection.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Leukocoria or new squint in a child: urgent ophthalmology referral.
- Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood.
- Early diagnosis can be vision- and life-saving.

questions.stem: Which pattern is more suggestive of hereditary retinoblastoma?
questions.correctAnswerText: Bilateral or multifocal disease
questions.initialExplanation: Hereditary retinoblastoma is associated with a germline RB1 pathogenic variant and is more likely to be bilateral or multifocal, often presenting at a younger age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Adult onset — Incorrect. Retinoblastoma is a childhood tumor.
- B. Down syndrome — Incorrect. This is not the characteristic association.

- C. Bilateral/multifocal — Correct. This pattern raises suspicion for hereditary disease.
- D. Hepatitis — Incorrect. There is no such defining association.
- E. Always unilateral — Incorrect. This is more typical of sporadic disease, although not absolute.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Hereditary retinoblastoma: germline RB1 variant, often bilateral/multifocal.
- First-degree relatives may need genetic counselling and ophthalmic surveillance based on family risk.
- Avoid assuming all unilateral cases are non-hereditary; genetics assessment may still be indicated.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an important differential diagnosis of leukocoria in a child?
questions.correctAnswerText: Congenital cataract
questions.initialExplanation: Leukocoria has several causes, including retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, retinopathy of prematurity, retinal detachment, and persistent fetal vasculature.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Otitis externa — Incorrect. This affects the external ear canal.
- B. Congenital cataract — Correct. It is a major differential diagnosis of a white pupillary reflex.
- C. Pityriasis rosea — Incorrect. This is a skin eruption.

- D. Scabies — Incorrect. This is a skin infestation.
- E. Allergic rhinitis — Incorrect. This affects the upper airway.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Leukocoria is a sign, not a diagnosis.
- Differential includes retinoblastoma, cataract, Coats disease, ROP, retinal detachment, and persistent fetal vasculature.
- All new leukocoria requires urgent specialist assessment.

questions.stem: Which finding is commonly associated with Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH)?

options.label: C
options.text: Hyperphagia and obesity as the finding

options.label: D
options.text: Osteolytic bone lesions, often involving the skull

questions.correctAnswerText: Osteolytic bone lesions, often involving the skull
questions.initialExplanation: LCH is a clonal myeloid disorder that can involve bone, skin, pituitary, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and bone marrow.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Molluscum — Incorrect. A centrally umbilicated papule is not a typical LCH bone lesion.

- B. Webbed neck — Incorrect. This is associated with Turner or Noonan phenotypes.
- C. Hyperphagia — Incorrect. This suggests other endocrine/genetic conditions.
- D. Osteolytic skull lesions — Correct. Bone is a frequent site of LCH involvement, and the skull is commonly affected.
- E. Rhinitis — Incorrect. This is not an LCH feature.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- LCH: bone pain/swelling, lytic lesions, skin rash, and possible systemic disease.
- Skull involvement may be associated with proptosis or diabetes insipidus if hypothalamic/pituitary structures are involved.
- Biopsy is important for diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which anatomical site is most characteristic of osteosarcoma?

options.label: C
options.text: Metaphysis of a long bone, commonly around the knee

questions.correctAnswerText: Metaphysis of a long bone, commonly around the knee
questions.initialExplanation: Osteosarcoma commonly arises in the metaphysis of long bones, particularly around the knee, in adolescents.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Disc — Incorrect. Osteosarcoma is a bone-forming malignancy, not a disc tumor.

- B. Diaphysis — Incorrect. This is more typical of Ewing sarcoma.
- C. Metaphysis around the knee — Correct. This is a classic site.
- D. Distal phalanx — Incorrect. This is not the characteristic site.
- E. Skull sutures — Incorrect. This is not typical.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Osteosarcoma: adolescent, metaphysis, local bone pain/swelling.
- Radiograph may show a sunburst pattern or Codman triangle.
- Evaluate persistent focal bone pain or swelling urgently.

questions.stem: Which radiographic pattern is classically associated with Ewing sarcoma?
questions.correctAnswerText: Onion-skin periosteal reaction
questions.initialExplanation: Ewing sarcoma commonly arises in the diaphysis of long bones and may produce an onion-skin periosteal reaction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Cupping/fraying — Incorrect. These are radiographic features of rickets.
- B. Sunburst — Incorrect. This is classically associated with osteosarcoma.
- C. Onion-skin — Correct. This is a classic radiographic pattern.
- D. Ground glass — Incorrect. This may be associated with fibrous dysplasia.
- E. Renal calcification — Incorrect. This is unrelated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ewing sarcoma: diaphysis, onion-skin appearance.
- Osteosarcoma: metaphysis, sunburst/Codman triangle.
- Both may cause pain, swelling, and systemic symptoms; diagnosis requires specialist imaging and biopsy.

questions.stem: Which comparison is correct?

options.label: B
options.text: Osteosarcoma usually arises in the metaphysis; Ewing sarcoma commonly arises in the diaphysis

options.label: C
options.text: Ewing sarcoma is diagnosed by serum AFP alone

options.label: D
options.text: Osteosarcoma arises in skin; Ewing in liver

questions.correctAnswerText: Osteosarcoma usually arises in the metaphysis; Ewing sarcoma commonly arises in the diaphysis
questions.initialExplanation: The anatomical distribution is a classic exam distinction, although real presentations require imaging and histopathological confirmation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Viral infection — Incorrect. Osteosarcoma is a malignancy.

- B. Metaphysis versus diaphysis — Correct. This is the key comparison.
- C. AFP — Incorrect. AFP is a marker used in selected liver/germ-cell tumors, not a diagnostic marker for Ewing sarcoma.
- D. Skin/liver — Incorrect. Both are malignant bone/soft tissue tumors, not organ-specific lesions as described.
- E. Benign — Incorrect. Both are malignant tumors.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Osteosarcoma: metaphysis, sunburst pattern.
- Ewing: diaphysis, onion-skin pattern.
- Persistent localized bone pain, swelling, or pathological fracture warrants urgent evaluation.

questions.stem: Which presentation should raise concern for a possible pediatric malignancy?

options.label: A
options.text: Persistent bone pain/swelling, pallor or bruising, lymphadenopathy, or an unexplained abdominal mass

options.label: B
options.text: A single mild episode of rhinorrhea

options.label: D
options.text: A short episode of uncomplicated diarrhea

questions.correctAnswerText: Persistent bone pain/swelling, pallor or bruising, lymphadenopathy, or an unexplained abdominal mass
questions.initialExplanation: Pediatric malignancies may present with nonspecific but persistent symptoms such as bone pain, weight loss, pallor, bruising, lymphadenopathy, or an abdominal mass.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Cancer warning features — Correct. Persistent or progressive unexplained findings require assessment.
- B. Rhinorrhea — Incorrect. A single mild upper respiratory symptom is common and nonspecific.
- C. Cradle cap — Incorrect. This is a benign infantile skin condition.
- D. Brief uncomplicated diarrhea — Incorrect. This is usually infectious and self-limited.
- E. Insect bite — Incorrect. A single local papule is not a typical malignancy warning sign.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Unexplained persistent symptoms deserve review.
- Red flags include weight loss, pallor, bruising, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, and masses.
- A well child with a persistent mass still requires appropriate investigation.

## Child Maltreatment, Neglect, and Safeguarding

questions.stem: Which statement best defines child maltreatment?

options.label: D
options.text: Physical, sexual, or psychological abuse, or neglect of a child by a parent, caregiver, or another responsible person

options.label: E
options.text: Any childhood illness that requires hospital admission

questions.correctAnswerText: Physical, sexual, or psychological abuse, or neglect of a child by a parent, caregiver, or another responsible person
questions.initialExplanation: Child maltreatment includes acts of commission (abuse) and acts of omission (neglect) that cause or risk harm to a child.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Accidental injury — Incorrect. Accidental injuries are not automatically abuse; history and consistency must be assessed.
- B. Congenital anomaly — Incorrect. A congenital anomaly is not by itself maltreatment.
- C. Normal behavior — Incorrect. Normal developmental behavior is not maltreatment.

- D. Abuse or neglect — Correct. This is the broad definition described.
- E. Hospital admission — Incorrect. Illness requiring admission is not itself maltreatment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Abuse = act of commission.
- Neglect = act of omission.
- Safeguarding focuses on the child's safety, health, dignity, and protection from future harm.

questions.stem: Which example best represents neglect rather than physical abuse?

options.label: E
options.text: Repeated failure to provide necessary medical care, nutrition, or safe supervision

questions.correctAnswerText: Repeated failure to provide necessary medical care, nutrition, or safe supervision
questions.initialExplanation: Neglect is failure to meet a child's basic physical, emotional, medical, educational, or supervisory needs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Intentional burn — Incorrect. This is physical abuse.
- B. Striking — Incorrect. This is physical abuse.
- C. Deliberate fracture — Incorrect. This is physical abuse.

- D. Shaking — Incorrect. This is physical abuse and can cause severe injury.
- E. Failure to provide care — Correct. This is an omission of necessary care.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neglect may involve medical, nutritional, educational, emotional, or supervisory needs.
- Consider whether the child's needs are consistently unmet and whether harm or risk is present.
- Poverty alone does not prove neglect; assess context, available support, and unmet needs.

questions.stem: Which statement about risk factors for child maltreatment is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Disability typically means a child is abused

options.label: B
options.text: Risk factors may involve the child, caregiver, family, and wider social environment

options.label: C
options.text: A single risk factor proves that abuse has occurred

options.label: D
options.text: Poverty alone is diagnostic of neglect

options.label: E
options.text: Risk assessment should ignore caregiver stress and social support

questions.correctAnswerText: Risk factors may involve the child, caregiver, family, and wider social environment
questions.initialExplanation: Risk factors are multidimensional and may include caregiver substance misuse, mental-health problems, domestic violence, social isolation, poverty, prematurity, disability, and family stress; none alone proves maltreatment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Disability means abuse — Incorrect. Disability may increase vulnerability but does not prove abuse.
- B. Multidimensional risks — Correct. Risk can arise from interactions between child, caregiver, family, and community factors.
- C. One factor proves abuse — Incorrect. Risk factors are not diagnostic evidence.
- D. Poverty is diagnostic — Incorrect. Poverty is a social risk and may require support; it is not proof of neglect.
- E. Ignore caregiver stress — Incorrect. Caregiver and social context are relevant to assessment and support planning.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider child-related, caregiver-related, and social/environmental factors.
- Avoid stereotypes or assumptions.
- Risk factors should trigger support and vigilance, not automatic conclusions.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant who is not yet independently mobile is found to have unexplained bruising. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: It is typically caused by a platelet disorder

options.label: B
options.text: Bruising is expected in each non-mobile infant

options.label: C
options.text: This is a concerning finding that requires prompt assessment for possible maltreatment and medical causes

options.label: D
options.text: It can be ignored if the infant is feeding well

options.label: E
options.text: It confirms abuse without further assessment

questions.correctAnswerText: This is a concerning finding that requires prompt assessment for possible maltreatment and medical causes
questions.initialExplanation: Unexplained bruising in a non-mobile infant is a significant safeguarding red flag, but assessment should also consider medical causes such as coagulation disorders.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Always platelet disorder — Incorrect. Bleeding disorders are part of the differential but should not be assumed.

- B. Expected bruising — Incorrect. Bruising is unusual in a non-mobile infant and requires explanation.
- C. Prompt assessment — Correct. The clinician should assess injury pattern, history, examination, medical differentials, and immediate safety.
- D. Ignore due to feeding — Incorrect. Normal feeding does not exclude injury.
- E. Abuse proven — Incorrect. Bruising raises concern but does not by itself establish a diagnosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Bruising in a non-mobile child is a red flag.
- Consider both inflicted injury and medical causes.
- Follow local safeguarding and child-protection pathways promptly.

source.raw: PDF p.25; NICE child maltreatment guidance

questions.stem: Which bruise pattern should raise particular concern for inflicted injury?

options.label: C
options.text: A single small bruise over a bony prominence in an independently mobile child with a consistent history

options.label: E
options.text: A bruise shaped like a hand, bite, ligature, or implement

questions.correctAnswerText: A bruise shaped like a hand, bite, ligature, or implement
questions.initialExplanation: Patterned bruising may reflect contact with an object or body part and should prompt assessment for possible inflicted injury.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Rash — Incorrect. This is not bruising.
- B. Birthmark — Incorrect. A congenital mark is not a bruise; document its appearance and history.
- C. Typical accidental bruise — Incorrect. A consistent history and location over a bony prominence may support accidental injury, though context still matters.
- D. Insect bite — Incorrect. This is a papule rather than patterned bruising.

- E. Patterned bruise — Correct. Hand, bite, ligature, grip, or implement-shaped bruising is concerning.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider shape, site, number, pattern, and developmental ability.
- Bruises on ears, neck, buttocks, eyes, or non-bony areas are concerning.
- Use a full examination and careful documentation.

questions.stem: Which history feature raises concern for possible non-accidental injury?

options.label: A
options.text: The injury is witnessed and independently corroborated

options.label: B
options.text: Caregivers seek prompt medical attention and provide a clear account

options.label: C
options.text: The history is consistent and matches the observed injury

options.label: D
options.text: The child has a known minor accidental mechanism that fits the examination

options.label: E
options.text: The explanation changes repeatedly or is inconsistent with the child's developmental abilities or injury pattern

questions.correctAnswerText: The explanation changes repeatedly or is inconsistent with the child's developmental abilities or injury pattern
questions.initialExplanation: Delay in seeking help, changing explanations, and a mechanism incompatible with the child's developmental ability are warning signs that require careful assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Witnessed/corroborated event — Incorrect. This may support the reported mechanism.
- B. Prompt care and clear account — Incorrect. This is generally reassuring but must be considered with all evidence.
- C. Consistent account — Incorrect. A consistent, plausible history may support an accidental mechanism, although it does not automatically exclude maltreatment.
- D. Plausible accidental mechanism — Incorrect. This is less concerning than a contradictory account.

- E. Inconsistent history — Correct. Discrepancy between history, developmental ability, and injury pattern raises concern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Assess timing, mechanism, developmental ability, and consistency.
- Document the exact words used by caregivers and child when relevant.
- Avoid accusatory or leading questioning.

questions.stem: Which burn pattern is particularly concerning for forced immersion injury?

options.label: A
options.text: A small irregular superficial burn on an exposed hand with a consistent accidental history

options.label: B
options.text: Symmetrical glove-and-stocking distribution with sharply demarcated margins

questions.correctAnswerText: Symmetrical glove-and-stocking distribution with sharply demarcated margins
questions.initialExplanation: Forced immersion may produce circumferential, symmetrical burns with clear lines of demarcation; this pattern warrants urgent safeguarding assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Small accidental burn — Incorrect. A plausible accidental pattern may be less concerning, but still requires context.
- B. Glove-and-stocking burns — Correct. This pattern is concerning for immersion in hot liquid.
- C. Insect bite — Incorrect. This is not a burn.
- D. Birthmark — Incorrect. This is not an injury.

- E. Sunburn — Incorrect. This is not an immersion pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider pattern, depth, distribution, and developmental ability.
- Forced immersion burns may be symmetrical and sharply demarcated.
- Provide urgent medical care and follow safeguarding protocols.

questions.stem: A young child has an unexplained fracture. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: A normal skin examination excludes non-accidental injury

options.label: B
options.text: Fracture pattern is not usually relevant

options.label: C
options.text: Osteogenesis imperfecta can be excluded without history or examination

options.label: D
options.text: Consider possible inflicted injury while also evaluating medical causes such as osteogenesis imperfecta and bone disease

options.label: E
options.text: most fractures in children prove abuse

questions.correctAnswerText: Consider possible inflicted injury while also evaluating medical causes such as osteogenesis imperfecta and bone disease
questions.initialExplanation: Unexplained fractures require an age- and mechanism-appropriate assessment, including possible maltreatment and medical conditions that predispose to fractures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Normal skin excludes injury — Incorrect. Serious internal injuries may occur without visible bruises.
- B. Pattern irrelevant — Incorrect. Fracture type, site, and age of injury can inform assessment but are not interpreted alone.

- C. Exclude osteogenesis imperfecta without assessment — Incorrect. Bone fragility disorders may need consideration.
- D. Balanced evaluation — Correct. The clinician must assess injury history, development, radiology, and differential diagnoses.
- E. All fractures prove abuse — Incorrect. Many pediatric fractures are accidental.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider inflicted injury and bone fragility disorders.
- Multiple fractures of different ages are concerning but require expert radiological interpretation.
- Do not rely on one finding in isolation.

questions.stem: In a young child with suspected physical abuse, what imaging investigation may be required to identify occult fractures?

options.label: D
options.text: Full skeletal survey according to age and safeguarding protocol

options.label: E
options.text: No imaging is ever indicated if there is no visible deformity

questions.correctAnswerText: Full skeletal survey according to age and safeguarding protocol
questions.initialExplanation: A skeletal survey may identify clinically occult fractures in young children when physical abuse is suspected; the decision and timing should follow specialist/local protocols.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Wrist only — Incorrect. This would miss injuries elsewhere.
- B. Ultrasound only — Incorrect. Ultrasound cannot replace skeletal imaging.
- C. Chest only — Incorrect. This is not a full assessment.
- D. Skeletal survey — Correct. It assesses multiple bones for occult injury in appropriate cases.
- E. No imaging — Incorrect. Occult fractures may be present without visible deformity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider skeletal survey in young children with suspected physical abuse according to protocol.
- CT or MRI may be needed when intracranial or other internal injury is suspected.
- Investigations should be coordinated with child-protection and pediatric radiology teams.

questions.stem: Which presentation in an infant should raise concern for possible abusive head trauma?

options.label: A
options.text: Unexplained seizures, vomiting, lethargy, apnea, bulging fontanelle, or altered consciousness

options.label: B
options.text: A single uncomplicated episode of hiccups

options.label: E
options.text: Mild nasal congestion without systemic symptoms

questions.correctAnswerText: Unexplained seizures, vomiting, lethargy, apnea, bulging fontanelle, or altered consciousness
questions.initialExplanation: Abusive head trauma may present with nonspecific neurological or respiratory deterioration; urgent assessment is required.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Neurological/respiratory deterioration — Correct. These may indicate serious intracranial injury.
- B. Hiccups — Incorrect. This is nonspecific and not a red flag alone.
- C. Molluscum — Incorrect. This is a superficial viral skin condition.

- D. Cradle cap — Incorrect. This is a benign skin condition.
- E. Nasal congestion — Incorrect. This does not indicate head injury by itself.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Abusive head trauma may present with altered consciousness, seizures, apnea, vomiting, or poor feeding.
- A normal external examination does not exclude intracranial injury.
- Stabilize first and arrange urgent specialist imaging/evaluation.

questions.stem: Which finding may indicate possible neglect when persistent and not adequately explained?

options.label: A
options.text: A parent asking questions about treatment

options.label: B
options.text: A child wearing ordinary play clothes

options.label: C
options.text: Repeatedly missed essential medical appointments and lack of necessary medical care

options.label: D
options.text: A child with a mild cold

options.label: E
options.text: One missed appointment due to a documented transport emergency

questions.correctAnswerText: Repeatedly missed essential medical appointments and lack of necessary medical care
questions.initialExplanation: Persistent failure to provide necessary healthcare, nutrition, hygiene, clothing, or supervision may indicate neglect and should trigger a supportive safeguarding assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Asking questions — Incorrect. This is appropriate caregiver engagement.

- B. Ordinary clothes — Incorrect. This is not evidence of neglect.
- C. Repeated lack of care — Correct. This is among the warning signs described.
- D. Mild cold — Incorrect. This is a common childhood illness.
- E. One explained missed appointment — Incorrect. A single event does not establish neglect; practical barriers should be explored.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider persistent unmet medical, nutritional, hygiene, clothing, emotional, or supervisory needs.
- Explore barriers such as transport, finances, and access to care.
- Safeguarding should be supportive and child-centered, not punitive or stereotype-driven.

questions.stem: Which statement is most appropriate when a child discloses possible sexual abuse?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeatedly interrogate the child until each detail is obtained

options.label: B
options.text: Dismiss the disclosure if the physical examination is normal

options.label: D
options.text: Confront the suspected perpetrator before arranging care

options.label: E
options.text: Listen calmly, take the disclosure seriously, avoid leading questions, document the child's words, and follow safeguarding pathways

questions.correctAnswerText: Listen calmly, take the disclosure seriously, avoid leading questions, document the child's words, and follow safeguarding pathways
questions.initialExplanation: A child's disclosure should be handled sensitively and safely; the clinician should avoid repeated or leading questioning and arrange specialist safeguarding assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Repeated interrogation — Incorrect. Repeated questioning can distress the child and affect the reliability of the account.
- B. Normal examination dismisses disclosure — Incorrect. A normal examination does not exclude sexual abuse.

- C. Absolute secrecy — Incorrect. Explain that information may need to be shared with professionals to keep the child safe.
- D. Confront suspected person — Incorrect. This may increase risk and compromise safeguarding.
- E. Child-centered response — Correct. It protects the child and preserves the integrity of any later investigation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Listen, reassure, avoid leading questions, and document exact words.
- Do not conduct a forensic interview outside your role.
- Arrange prompt specialist safeguarding/child protection assessment and consider urgent medical needs.

questions.correctAnswerText: A caregiver fabricates symptoms or deliberately induces illness, leading to unnecessary medical assessment or harm
questions.initialExplanation: Fabricated or induced illness describes situations where a caregiver invents, exaggerates, or deliberately causes symptoms or signs in a child, potentially exposing the child to harm.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Allergic rash — Incorrect. This is a genuine possible medical condition.

- B. Accurate symptom report — Incorrect. This is normal caregiving.
- C. Genetic disease — Incorrect. This is a medical disorder, not fabricated illness.
- D. Fabrication/induction — Correct. This includes false reports and deliberate production of symptoms or illness.
- E. Viral fever — Incorrect. This is a common genuine illness.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider fabricated/induced illness when accounts, observations, and objective findings are repeatedly inconsistent.
- Protect the child and coordinate a multidisciplinary safeguarding response.
- Avoid premature accusations; document objectively and escalate concerns appropriately.

options.label: C

questions.correctAnswerText: Ensure the child's immediate safety, treat urgent injuries, document findings, and activate the safeguarding pathway
questions.initialExplanation: Management prioritizes stabilization and safety, followed by appropriate investigations, careful documentation, multidisciplinary assessment, and action according to local child-protection law and policy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Safety and safeguarding — Correct. The child must be medically stabilized and protected from further harm.
- B. Avoid MDT — Incorrect. A multidisciplinary approach is essential in complex cases.

- C. Wait for admission — Incorrect. Safeguarding action does not depend on an admission.
- D. Immediate discharge — Incorrect. This may expose the child to further risk.
- E. Confrontation — Incorrect. This may increase risk and compromise the assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Stabilize and assess immediate risk.
- Document injuries objectively, using body maps/photos according to policy and consent.
- Arrange appropriate investigations and specialist review.
- Follow local reporting and safeguarding requirements.
- Plan a safe disposition before discharge.

questions.stem: A child develops generalized urticaria, wheeze, stridor and hypotension minutes after a food exposure. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.correctAnswerText: Intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine)
questions.initialExplanation: This is anaphylaxis with airway, breathing and circulatory involvement; IM adrenaline is first-line.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect: Inhaled corticosteroids do not reverse acute anaphylaxis.
- B. Incorrect: Untreated anaphylaxis can rapidly deteriorate.

- C. Correct: IM adrenaline is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.
- D. Incorrect: Antihistamines may help skin symptoms but do not treat life-threatening airway or circulatory compromise.
- E. Incorrect: Antibiotics are not indicated for an immediate allergic reaction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Recognize multisystem anaphylaxis and give IM adrenaline promptly.
- Support airway, breathing and circulation; arrange emergency monitoring and further care.

questions.stem: A child with acute hepatitis develops encephalopathy and a markedly prolonged prothrombin time that does not correct after vitamin K. Which complication should be suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Acute liver failure
questions.initialExplanation: Encephalopathy with significant coagulopathy not corrected by vitamin K indicates acute liver failure in a child.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect: Uncomplicated hepatitis does not include this degree of synthetic failure and encephalopathy.
- B. Incorrect: Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without liver failure.
- C. Incorrect: Haemolysis does not account for hepatic synthetic failure.

- D. Correct: The combination indicates loss of hepatic synthetic function and encephalopathy.
- E. Incorrect: Cholestasis alone does not explain encephalopathy with uncorrected coagulopathy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Acute liver failure is a time-critical emergency requiring urgent specialist/PICU referral.
- Monitor glucose, coagulation, encephalopathy and complications.

questions.stem: A child has chronic liver disease, neuropsychiatric changes and a Kayser–Fleischer ring. Which disorder should be considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Wilson disease
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance associates Wilson disease with hepatic and neurological manifestations and Kayser–Fleischer rings.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect: Gilbert syndrome causes benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
- B. Incorrect: Biliary atresia presents in infancy with persistent conjugated jaundice.
- C. Incorrect: Acute hepatitis A is an acute infection, not a chronic copper storage disorder.

- D. Incorrect: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency may cause liver/lung disease but not the classic Kayser–Fleischer ring.
- E. Correct: Wilson disease causes copper accumulation with hepatic and neurological disease.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Wilson disease: assess copper metabolism and involve specialist hepatology.
- Kayser–Fleischer rings are a high-yield association.

questions.stem: A parent notices a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) in a young child. Which tumor is the key diagnosis to exclude urgently?
questions.correctAnswerText: Retinoblastoma
questions.initialExplanation: Leukocoria is a classic warning sign of retinoblastoma and requires urgent ophthalmological assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect: Neuroblastoma usually presents with an abdominal/adrenal mass or systemic symptoms.
- B. Correct: Retinoblastoma arises in the retina and may present with leukocoria.
- C. Incorrect: Wilms tumor presents as an abdominal renal mass.
- D. Incorrect: Osteosarcoma causes bone pain/swelling.

- E. Incorrect: Hepatoblastoma presents as a liver mass.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Leukocoria is a red flag: urgent ophthalmology assessment is needed.
- Retinoblastoma may be unilateral or bilateral and can be life-threatening.
